title: Two Times In the 70s When People Buried Ferraris
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant cover two 1970s cases of Ferraris being buried. First, socialite Sandra West (widow of Texas oil heir Ike West) was buried in her 1964 Ferrari 330 America in San Antonio, per her wishes, after dying in 1977; a judge ordered the burial carried out despite her lawyer's objections. Second, a Dino 246 GTS reported stolen by Rosando Cruz was found buried in West Athens, Los Angeles, in the 1970s; the story was long told as kids finding it, but it was actually a tip from a confidential informant, and the theft is believed to have been staged for an insurance claim. The car was later restored and is still owned by a collector. The episode also includes a few opening tour announcements and a listener mail segment about the How the Sun Works rerun/select episode and a teacher's note.

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts announce Australia and New Zealand tour dates in September, then banter about Washington DC legal weed, Magnum P.I. and Ferraris, and their own cars.

segments.title: Sandra West and her 1964 Ferrari 330 America
segments.summary: Sandra West, a Beverly Hills socialite, married Texas oil heir Ike West after he was estranged in Mexico. She bought a 1964 Ferrari 330 America; Ike died in Las Vegas at the Flamingo Hotel under mysterious circumstances. Sandra inherited his share of the fortune and later dated Engelbert Humperdinck and collected Ferraris.

segments.title: Sandra West's death and burial wish
segments.summary: Sandra died in 1977 of an overdose of codeine and barbiturates after a car wreck. Years earlier she had written that she wanted to be buried in her Ferrari, in her nightgown, seated reclined. Her brother-in-law Saul West was tasked with carrying this out, and the judge ruled the burial must proceed despite a psychiatrist describing her as paranoid. The car was put in a giant casket and buried by crane in San Antonio before about 300 spectators.

segments.title: Discovery of buried Dino in West Athens
segments.summary: Detectives Dennis Carroll and Joe Sabbath dug up a Ferrari Dino 246 GTS in West Athens, Los Angeles. Priscilla Paynton of the LA Times reported the car was in surprisingly good condition and mistakenly named Carroll as Lenny Carroll. The car was reported stolen in 1974 from outside the Brown Derby after owner Rosando Cruz parked on Wilshire Boulevard.

segments.title: Car condition, auction, and restoration
segments.summary: The car was in poor shape with rust and damage, though thieves had stuffed towels in the intake. Farmers Insurance displayed it in Pasadena, where parts were stripped, then sold it for a low price to a Burbank mechanic. It later resurfaced restored and licensed as 'dug up' before disappearing from registries.

segments.title: True story: informant tip and staged theft
segments.summary: Mike Spinelli of Jalopnik learned from Dennis Carroll that the kids-digging story was invented to protect a confidential informant, a heroin addict who tipped police. The hosts argue Cruz likely staged the theft to collect insurance and escape payments, though he was never charged. The car survived partly because of a Southern California drought.

segments.title: Car owner today and wrap-up
segments.summary: Brad Howard owns the restored car today. The hosts close the buried-car topic and invite listeners to send other buried-car cases.

segments.title: Listener mail: teacher and How the Sun Works rerun
segments.summary: A teacher named Hannah Barton wrote that she first heard the How the Sun Works episode, which the hosts had selected for rerun, and that the show has been part of her life; she now teaches seventh and eighth grade. The hosts thank her and invite teachers to share their classes.
